Another German state plans switch back from Linux to Windows

Linux needs to be overhauled completely to make it a viable desktop OS for general business and home use. While it is great for tech people and others who like to get their hands dirty, Linux fails miserably at handling business and semi-pro users who need computers but have other areas to focus on besides learning an OS. To succeed with these groups of business users, Linux needs a working base of subsystems that provide consistent results including printing, display, sound, networking and storage management. Until there is a stable, viable and reliable common set of subsystems for programmers to work with, business and professional software on Linux will remain niche and isolated. Windows has provided these subsystems and their associated APIs for a very long time which gives programmers the necessary base to build on and not have to worry about compatibility. Linux needs this desperately. It needs this to survive in the non-tech, non-server world. Fix this core set of problems and then we can finally see the Year of the Linux Desktop. Until then expect Linux to continue to fall flat for business and professional environments that aren't tech related.

Application devs also desperately need to modernize their UI's. If I demoed Thunderbird to a company I would be laughed out of the room.

Printing is a rough nut because the vendors would need to provide full feature drivers. While you can certainly ky print to many things, not being able to select stapling and other advanced features is a bag of hurt.

Lastly, a Google play style store where applications can be loaded to many distros without a lot of hassle. This is why Android and all its fragmentation actually works.

More good points. Linux devs are generally accepting of bad user interface design because it's less important how it looks/works than the fact that it's free. General and business users have an expectation of polish and fit that needs a good UI/UX. Thunderbird is an excellent example of a product that does its job but looks like garbage. LibreOffice too. They lose points automatically because users see them as antiquated and less featured, which often they are.

Yeah printing will require the OEMs to get on board. They won't because their cash cow is ink sales and there is no significant Linux userbase of normies who print to sell to. This will be a huge stumbling block for Linux for a long time. Open Source Hardware will be of no use here either because printing in general is a tough technical area. Unless the world can be happy switching back to impact printing (dot matrix and daisy wheel), inkjet and laser printing in the DIY world is not going to happen. Sure there are some DIY inkjet printers out there, but all of them rely on using print heads/cartridges from the printer makers so they are not a solution at all.

App store- a total must have. Repos and package managers are no substitute for a proper app store where casual users can easily get and install software. The current methods suffer from the same problems as the UI/UX issue- the devs think this is good enough so they won't improve it. Also, having too many people/devs involved in the whole thing makes Linux a "design by committee" disaster. No one distro works for everyone and no one wants to make a distro that caters to non-technical users. This combined with the app ecosystem problems will keep the year of the Linux desktop forever a dream.
